chapter: Stallings ch 1 — Basic Concepts and Computer Evolution
note: Every stem, key and rationale here is grounded in docs/source/book/ch-01.md. Where the book gives an example verbatim (the multiply instruction, the System/370 family) the item uses that example rather than inventing a parallel one.

items.stem: In Stallings' terms, computer ARCHITECTURE refers to which attributes of a system?
items.correct: Those visible to the programmer, having a direct impact on the logical execution of a program
distractors: The operational units and their interconnections that realise the specification
The hardware details deliberately kept transparent to the programmer
The physical layout of components on the motherboard
items.rationale: Architecture is what a program can SEE: instruction set, data type widths, I/O mechanisms, addressing. The second option is the definition of organization, and the third is the distractor that mistakes 'architecture' for physical construction.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.1 — 'attributes of a system visible to a programmer'

items.stem: Computer ORGANIZATION refers to which of the following?
items.correct: The operational units and their interconnections that realise the architectural specification
distractors: The attributes that have a direct impact on the logical execution of a program
The instruction formats, opcodes and registers available to a programmer
The set of programming languages a machine is able to compile
items.rationale: Organization is HOW the architecture is realised — control signals, peripheral interfaces, memory technology. The first two options are both descriptions of architecture, and the second is specifically the ISA.

items.stem: The term 'instruction set architecture' (ISA) is often used interchangeably with which term?
distractors: Computer organization
Microarchitecture
System interconnection
items.rationale: The ISA defines instruction formats, opcodes, registers, and the effect of instructions on registers and memory — all programmer-visible, which is exactly what architecture means. Microarchitecture describes the organizational realisation, which is the opposite side of the distinction.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.1 — 'often used interchangeably with computer architecture'

items.stem: Deciding WHETHER a computer will have a multiply instruction is which kind of design issue?
items.correct: Architectural — it changes what a program can express
distractors: Organizational — it concerns how the hardware is built
Neither: instruction selection is a compiler concern
Both equally, since every instruction needs hardware
items.rationale: Stallings uses this exact example. WHETHER the instruction exists is architectural, because a programmer can see it. WHETHER it is implemented by a dedicated multiply unit or by repeated use of the adder is organizational, and that second decision turns on expected frequency of use, relative speed, cost and physical size.

items.stem: Which of the following is an ORGANIZATIONAL attribute rather than an architectural one?
distractors: The number of bits used to represent a character
The I/O mechanisms available to a program
The techniques available for addressing memory
items.rationale: Stallings lists memory technology, control signals and peripheral interfaces as organizational — hardware details transparent to the programmer. The three distractors are his examples of ARCHITECTURAL attributes, all of which a program can observe.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.1 — the two lists of example attributes

items.stem: A manufacturer offers several models sharing one architecture but differing in organization, as IBM did with the System/370. What does this arrangement buy the customer?
items.correct: They can move to a faster, dearer model later without abandoning software already written
distractors: Each model can run a different instruction set suited to its price point
Software written for a faster model runs unchanged only if recompiled for the slower one
The models share a price and differ only in physical size
items.rationale: Software compatibility follows the ARCHITECTURE, and every model in the family shares it. Organization is what varies, which is why the models differ in price and performance. If the instruction sets differed, as the first distractor claims, the compatibility the family exists to provide would be gone.

items.stem: Stallings reduces everything a computer does to four basic functions. Which set is correct?
items.correct: Data processing, data storage, data movement, and control
distractors: Input, processing, output, and feedback
Fetch, decode, execute, and write back
Arithmetic, logic, branching, and interrupt handling
items.rationale: The four functions are the top-level view. 'Fetch, decode, execute' is the instruction cycle — a level down, and covered in chapter 3 — and the other two options are plausible-sounding groupings the book never uses.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — 'only four basic functions that a computer can perform'

items.stem: A digital computer is built from just two fundamental component types. Which basic function does each provide?
items.correct: Gates provide data processing; memory cells provide data storage
distractors: Gates provide data storage; memory cells provide data processing
Gates provide control; memory cells provide data movement
Gates provide data movement; memory cells provide control
items.rationale: A gate implements a Boolean function, which is processing. A memory cell holds one bit in one of two stable states, which is storage. Movement is provided by the PATHS between components, and control by the signals those paths carry — neither is a component type of its own.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.5 — gates and memory cells mapped to the four functions

items.stem: Stallings quotes Siewiorek: 'There is remarkably little shaping of computer structure to fit the function to be performed.' What accounts for this?
items.correct: Computers are general purpose, so functional specialisation happens at programming time rather than design time
distractors: The four basic functions are too simple to require any specialised structure
Manufacturing constraints make specialised structures too expensive to build
Specialised structures were abandoned once integrated circuits arrived
items.rationale: The quotation's own explanation is the general-purpose nature of computers: the same hardware serves every application because the specialisation is supplied later, by a program. The other options offer economic or historical reasons the passage does not give.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — the [SIEW82] quotation and its gloss

items.stem: Data movement to a device directly attached to the computer is called input-output. What is the same function called when the data travels to a REMOTE device instead?
distractors: Direct memory access
Peripheral transfer
Long-term data storage
items.rationale: Stallings splits data movement by distance: a directly connected device is a peripheral and the process is I/O; over longer distances the same function is called data communications. Direct memory access is a technique for performing I/O, not a category of movement.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — data movement, I/O versus data communications

items.stem: A keystroke travels from the keyboard into main memory. Put the components it passes through in order, from the outside in.
items.rationale: The peripheral hands data to the I/O module, which is the computer's interface to the external environment. The system bus carries it between the major components, and main memory is where it comes to rest. This is the top-level structure of Figure 1.1 traced along one operation.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — Figure 1.1 top-level structure, and the I/O definition

items.stem: A computer receives a file over the network and writes it to its hard disk. Which pair of basic functions does this operation chiefly exercise?
distractors: Data processing and control only
Data processing and data movement
Control and data storage only
items.rationale: Arriving over a network is data movement — data communications, since the source is remote — and writing to disk is long-term data storage. Nothing about the contents is transformed, so data processing is not the operation's substance even though the processor is involved in carrying it out.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — the four functions and the possible operations they compose

items.stem: What are the four main structural components of a traditional single-processor computer?
items.correct: CPU, main memory, I/O, and system interconnection
distractors: Control unit, ALU, registers, and CPU interconnection
CPU, cache, main memory, and secondary storage
Processor, motherboard, expansion boards, and chips
items.rationale: These are the top-level four. The first distractor is the correct answer to a DIFFERENT question — those are the major structural components of the CPU, one level down — and confusing the two levels is the commonest error on this material.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — 'There are four main structural components'

items.stem: Figure 1.1 nests the computer's structure. Put these in order from the outermost enclosing level to the innermost.
items.rationale: The computer contains the CPU alongside memory, I/O and the interconnection. The CPU contains the control unit alongside the ALU and registers. The control unit, in a microprogrammed implementation, contains sequencing logic together with its registers, decoders and control memory. Each level is a component of the one before it.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — Figure 1.1, The Computer: Top-Level Structure

items.stem: Under the terminology Stallings adopts, what distinguishes a PROCESSOR from a CORE?
items.correct: A processor is the physical piece of silicon, which may contain one or more cores
distractors: A core is the physical chip; a processor is one execution unit within it
They are interchangeable terms for the same component
A processor executes instructions; a core only holds cache
items.rationale: The processor is the physical silicon containing one or more cores; a core is an individual processing unit on that chip, functionally equivalent to a CPU on a single-CPU system. The first distractor inverts the two, which is the error the book's terminology note exists to prevent.
items.source: ch-01.md §1.2 — the CPU / core / processor definitions
